nodes.label: Cache-aside as an interview story
nodes.rationale: Jackson over JDK serialization because it is portable, human-readable in redis-cli, and has no serialVersionUID landmines. Cache-aside rather than write-through because the source of truth is an external API with no write path to intercept; when Redis is down it degrades to slow-but-correct.

nodes.label: Atomic check-then-act in Redis via Lua
nodes.rationale: Redis is single-threaded and runs a Lua script as one indivisible unit, so the read and write cannot be split. INCR is atomic but GET+SET is not.

nodes.label: Thundering herd / cache stampede
nodes.rationale: If the lock winner dies, the PX expiry releases the lock and a loser becomes the next winner — which is why SETNX is never used without a TTL.

nodes.label: Redis vs Kafka in the same system
nodes.rationale: Redis holds ephemeral shared state (cache, counters, locks); Kafka carries durable work that must survive restarts. Losing Redis costs performance; losing Kafka costs research runs.

nodes.label: CompletableFuture default executor pitfall
nodes.rationale: The default ForkJoinPool.commonPool is sized for CPU-bound work and is wrong for blocking IO, so an explicit executor is passed — newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor here.

nodes.label: Semaphore vs fixed thread pool
nodes.rationale: A pool bounds threads; a semaphore bounds concurrent access to a resource. With virtual threads you have effectively unlimited threads, so the semaphore does the real work. Release in finally or the leaked permit shows up hours later as unexplained slowness.

nodes.label: Virtual threads: when they help
nodes.rationale: They help when blocked on IO, which is ~95% of this project's wall clock, and do nothing for CPU-bound work. synchronized blocks used to pin a virtual thread to its carrier — use ReentrantLock instead.

nodes.label: Distributed vs in-process coordination
nodes.rationale: Called the project's best system-design answer: an AtomicInteger is correct within one JVM and wrong the moment there are two replicas or a restart. Coordinate across instances with a shared store that has atomic operations, never in-memory primitives.

nodes.label: The fan-in race condition war story
nodes.rationale: Two researchers finish simultaneously, both read completed = 5 and both write 6 — either nobody sees equality or both dispatch the writer twice. UPDATE ... SET completed = completed + 1 ... RETURNING makes read and write one atomic statement so exactly one caller observes equality.

nodes.label: Thread pool sizing and CountDownLatch harness
nodes.rationale: CPU-bound ~= cores, IO-bound much higher or virtual threads; the benchmark sweeps concurrency 1->12 for a real curve. CountDownLatch starts all threads simultaneously so contention rather than ramp-up is measured.

nodes.label: Theory the project does not teach
nodes.rationale: Java memory model, ConcurrentHashMap internals, deadlock conditions, ReentrantLock semantics, ThreadLocal leaks, and Redis persistence must be read separately. The project gives stories, not coverage; interviews want both.

nodes.label: Immutable SHA image tags over :latest
nodes.rationale: Rollback is impossible against a moving pointer and 'what is running right now' becomes unanswerable; SHA tags make rollback one line and give a free audit trail.

nodes.label: Migrations must be backward-compatible with the previous image
nodes.rationale: Flyway takes a lock on startup so concurrent starts are safe, but a rollback breaks unless changes are additive — never drop a column in the same release that stops using it.

nodes.label: Shared common module vs schema-first contracts
nodes.rationale: Deliberate coupling: Spring AI binds LLM output straight to these records so a writer/critic mismatch is a compile error. The purist alternative (JSON Schema or Protobuf on the wire) is right once independent teams ship on independent schedules. Right call for one team's release cadence, wrong the moment there are two.

nodes.label: Monorepo over polyrepo
nodes.rationale: Polyrepo solves team decoupling; one person writing both ends of every contract has no team to decouple from, so it would just mean four clones, four CI setups, and hand-bumping a shared jar.

nodes.label: Where auth lives and where it does not
nodes.rationale: The honest answer to 'how did you secure inter-service communication' is: I didn't expose them. Knowing when not to add a security layer is framed as the more senior answer.

nodes.label: OAuth2 client vs authorization server
nodes.rationale: Google issues the token and we validate it; we never store a password. Candidates routinely say 'I implemented OAuth2' meaning they added a login button — know which side of the line you're on.

nodes.label: Why no Eureka (LEARNING.md)
nodes.rationale: Kubernetes provides service discovery natively and Compose resolves by service name, so Eureka duplicates a platform feature and is a recognized anti-pattern. Spring Cloud Netflix's Ribbon, Hystrix and Zuul are in maintenance mode, superseded by Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, Resilience4j and Spring Cloud Gateway.

nodes.label: Why KEDA on only one service (LEARNING.md)
nodes.rationale: agent-service is genuinely bursty and scales on Kafka consumer lag; retrieval-service and control-plane get fixed replicas because their load is steady. Autoscaling everything is cargo culting — being able to say why one service and not three is the point.
